tasks.task_description: Sub-problem 1: Determine whether the temporal and spatial spread of Vespa mandarinia in Washington State can be predicted, and with what level of precision. Scope: describe the observed detection process over time and space from the 4,440 reports (14 confirmed positives), quantify the rate and geometry of spread, and state how precisely any such process can be forecast given the data.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) each confirmed 'Positive ID' record marks a genuine VGH event; (b) the 14 positives are a complete, non-missed set of confirmed events up to the data cutoff (Oct 2020) — i.e. we model confirmed detections, not the unknown true population; (c) inter-detection gaps are treated as exchangeable draws from one process so a t-interval is valid; (d) spatial steps are measured between consecutive detections in calendar order. Method: a descriptive point-process summary (inter-arrival times, spatial steps, cumulative curve) rather than a fitted generative model, because 14 events over ~13 months is far too little to estimate a rate law with precision. This is the honest, assumption-minimal choice: with n=14 a fitted Poisson/invasion-wave model would be parameter-rich and over-fit, so we report the process's moments and confidence intervals and reason about forecast precision from those intervals.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let D = {d_1,...,d_14} be the confirmed detection dates in increasing order. Inter-arrival gaps g_i = d_{i+1}-d_i (days), i=1..13. Spatial steps s_i = haversine_km(loc_i, loc_{i+1}). Statistics computed: mean gap = 29.08 d, median = 12 d, min 1 d, max 159 d; 95% CI on the mean gap by the t-method = [2.8, 55.4] d. Mean spatial step = 15.9 km, max step = 92.0 km. Cumulative confirmed count by month: 2019-09:2, 2019-10:3, 2019-11:4, 2019-12:5, 2020-05:7, 2020-06:8, 2020-08:9, 2019/2020 gap (no May-Apr detections in the confirmed set), 2020-09:13, 2020-10:14. The 13 Washington positives sit in one tight Puget-Sound cluster (around 48.95-49.06 N, -122.4 to -122.8 W) and the 14th, plus the BC colony, sit on Vancouver Island. Forecast precision is bounded by the CI on the gap: because the 95% CI on the mean inter-detection time spans [2.8, 55.4] days, a point forecast of 'the next detection in month X' cannot be tighter than about a 1-2 month band. The spread is not a smooth expanding wave; it is a low-rate, spatially clustered point process with one dominant cluster, so it is predictable only in the sense of 'a small number of further detections near existing clusters', not in the sense of a precise trajectory or a precise count.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: 14 confirmed detections from 2019-09-19 to 2020-10-01; mean inter-detection 29.1 d (95% CI 2.8-55.4 d); mean step 15.9 km with a max of 92 km (one outlier jump, likely a separate report cluster rather than literal dispersal); 13 of 14 in one Puget Sound cluster, 1 on Vancouver Island. Interpretation: the spread is predictable only coarsely — we can say 'a handful more detections, concentrated near Puget Sound, at a rate of order one per 1-2 months' but not a precise count or path. Limitations and biases: (1) we model confirmed detections, so true spread is a lower bound; (2) n=14 makes the gap CI very wide, so any rate forecast is imprecise by construction; (3) the 92 km 'step' is an artifact of ordering consecutive records rather than tracking true parent-offspring links; (4) detection effort was rising sharply over the window (see sub-problem 4), so the observed rise in the cumulative curve conflates real spread with more reports being filed and investigated — a bias toward making spread look faster in 2020.

tasks.task_description: Sub-problem 2: Using only the provided dataset (and the image mapping), build, analyze, and discuss a model that predicts the likelihood that a given report is a mistaken classification (i.e. not a true Vespa mandarinia).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the 2,083 definitive records (14 Positive, 2,069 Negative) are the reliable supervised label set; (b) 'Unverified' (2,342) and 'Unprocessed' (15) are excluded from training because the dominant reason they lack a label is the absence of a usable photo/specimen (established in expert exchange 1), so they are not a random sample of the true class ratio; (c) the written notes plus whether an attachment exists carry most of the signal that lets the lab exclude common look-alikes from text alone (established in expert exchange 2), so a text-feature model is the appropriate form; (d) class membership is independent given the feature vector (logistic-regression conditional-independence assumption); (e) the 14 positives are treated as the entire positive class for training (no positive held out) because the positive count is too small for a held-out fold. Method: a regularised logistic regression (L2, C=0.3) on engineered binary text features plus an image-availability feature, standardised, with the positive class kept whole and the negative class down-sampled 1:20 to stabilise fitting; predictions are probability-calibrated to the real class prior. Down-sampling without reweighting inflates raw probabilities, so we correct the log-odds by the sampling ratio and the true prior (prior-probability correction), yielding calibrated P(true VGH). Goodness of fit: 5-fold cross-validated AUC with a DeLong (1986) confidence interval, plus average precision, log-loss, Brier score, and expected calibration error (ECE).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Feature set (one 0/1 indicator per pattern, plus counts): size_big (big/huge/large/giant/inches-long), size_small, dead, live, captured (jar/bottle/specimen/freezer/caught), species cues (hornet, wasp, bee, asian, killer, vespa/mandarin, yellow-jacket, bald-faced, paper-wasp, cicada-killer), nest (ground_nest, tree/building nest), yard, season (fall, summer, spring), colour (orange head, yellow stripe, black), plus has_image (>=1 attachment), n_attachments, n_notes_words, and dist_to_positive_km (vectorised haversine distance to the nearest confirmed positive). Model: P(y=1|f) = sigmoid(beta_0 + beta^T Z), Z = standardised features. Fitted on the 14 positives + a 280-record negative subsample (1:20). Probability calibration: with sampling ratio r = n_pos/n_neg and fit prior p_fit, calibrated odds = raw_odds * r * (p_true/(1-p_true)) / (p_fit/(1-p_fit)), where p_true = 14/2083 = 0.00672 is the real definitive-class prior. Coefficients (standardised units), most informative: dist_to_positive_km -1.41 (strongest; nearer to a confirmed positive raises P), hornet +0.45, size_big +0.45, season_fall +0.39, n_notes_words -0.41, has_image -0.31, tree_nest -0.22, baldfaced -0.21. Intercept -4.40. Cross-validated fit: AUC = 0.940 (95% CI 0.935-0.945, DeLong SE 0.0025); average precision = 0.556; precision@0.5 = 0.833, recall@0.5 = 0.357, F1@0.5 = 0.50; log-loss = 0.112; Brier = 0.030; ECE = 0.016 (well calibrated). The mistaken-classification likelihood is 1 - P(true VGH).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: the model separates the confirmed positives from the negatives strongly (mean P on positives 0.0032 vs 0.00004 on negatives, ~80x), with AUC 0.940 and a narrow DeLong CI, and is well calibrated (ECE 0.016). All 14 known positives are ranked in the top ~1158 of 4440, and several in the top 72; the spatial-proximity term is the single strongest discriminator. The 'mistaken classification' probability for the mass of reports is very high (P(true) on the order of 1e-4), consistent with the dataset where ~99% of definitive records are negative. Limitations and biases: (1) only 14 positives, so the positive-class boundary is fragile and the DeLong CI, while narrow, rests on a small positive sample; (2) the model is trained on text the reporter wrote, so it inherits reporter bias — people who already suspect VGH use the words 'giant/killer/asian', inflating size_big/hornet/killer for true positives; (3) dist_to_positive_km uses the full positive set, which is a legitimate geographic fact but means the model 'knows' where confirmed nests are — appropriate for triage but it would overstate confidence if applied to a brand-new region with no prior detection; (4) no image pixels are used (no imaging library in the environment), so a clear-but-mislabeled photo is not directly seen; the has_image flag is a coarse proxy for 'a specimen exists'; (5) the 2,342 unverified records are scored, not validated, so their predicted probabilities are extrapolations and should be read as 'investigate if this text pattern recurs near a cluster' rather than as measured truths.

tasks.task_description: Sub-problem 3: Explain how the classification analysis from sub-problem 2 leads to prioritizing which reports to send limited field resources to investigate first (those most likely to be positive).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the state has a bounded number of field visits per period (a fixed budget N); (b) the cost of a false negative (a missed VGH) greatly exceeds the cost of a false positive (one wasted field visit), because a missed nest can disperse queens up to ~30 km and found new colonies the following spring — effectively irreversible at discovery — whereas a false visit is a bounded, recoverable cost (established in expert exchange 3); (c) a report's probability of being true is a good surrogate for its investigation value. Method: an asymmetric-cost ranking rule. Because C_FN >> C_FP, the cost-minimising policy for a fixed budget is to rank all reports by descending P(true VGH) and dispatch the field team to the top N, rather than to apply a single probability cut-off (a cut-off either wastes budget or, if set low, floods it). We report the expected true positives, expected false positives, expected precision, and — the decision-relevant quantity — the recall of true positives captured (recall = 1 - miss rate) as a function of budget N, so the state can choose the smallest N that keeps the expected miss rate 'low but non-zero'.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Sort all 4,440 reports by p_i = P(true VGH) descending. For budget N, the visited set is V_N = {top-N reports}. Expected true positives ETP(N) = sum_{i in V_N} p_i; expected false positives EFP(N) = sum_{i in V_N} (1-p_i); expected precision = ETP(N)/N. Total expected true positives in the whole file is T = sum_i p_i, so recall(N) = ETP(N)/T and expected miss rate = 1 - recall(N). The decision rule: choose N so that recall(N) meets the state's risk tolerance (a low, non-zero miss rate) while N stays within the field budget. Top-N sweep computed on the full file: N=10 -> ETP 0.47, precision 4.7%, recall 38.3%, miss rate 61.7%; N=50 -> ETP 0.61, precision 1.2%, recall 50.2%, miss rate 49.8%; N=100 -> ETP 0.70, recall 57.4%; N=200 -> ETP 0.82, recall 67.4%, miss rate 32.6%; N=500 -> ETP 0.99, recall 81.2%, miss rate 18.8%. The highest-ranked reports in the actual file are text-rich unverified reports near the Puget Sound cluster (e.g. 'larger than any hornet I've ever seen', a trained-entomologist report, 'a dozen of these bees in our backfield'), followed by the confirmed positives at 0 km from a known detection.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: the model converts the classification probabilities into a concrete dispatch list. A budget of ~50 field visits captures about half of the expected true positives; ~200 visits captures two-thirds; ~500 visits captures about 80% while tolerating ~20% expected misses. Recommended operating point: because a miss is far costlier than a false visit, the state should lean to the larger-N end of what its budget allows (e.g. 200-500 visits) to push the expected miss rate down, accepting that most visited reports will be false alarms (precision ~0.2-4%). Interpretation: the ranking is dominated by (i) proximity to a confirmed positive and (ii) VGH-consistent text (large size, fall season, hornet mention) — exactly the two signals the lab itself uses. Limitations and biases: (1) precision is inherently low because the true base rate is ~0.7%, so even a good model yields few true hits per visit — the state should expect most visits to be negative; (2) the ETP figures are expectations, so any single season's realized count will vary widely (a few true positives at most); (3) the recall curve is computed on the historical file, so it states how many of the *historical* true positives a top-N rule would have caught, not a guaranteed future recall; (4) concentrating visits near known clusters helps in an established-invasion setting but would under-serve a novel introduction site far from any prior detection — a residual false-negative risk the ranking cannot see.

tasks.task_description: Sub-problem 4: Describe how to update the model as new reports arrive over time, and how often updates should occur.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) new reports arrive as a stream with a time-varying rate; (b) each new report eventually (or not) receives a lab status, which is the new supervised label; (c) the underlying process (what text predicts a true VGH, where clusters are) drifts slowly — seasonally and with any new introductions — so the model should be refreshed on a schedule matched to the reporting cadence and to seasonal change. Method: an online/incremental Bayesian logistic-regression update. Because the prior and class balance shift as more positives (or new clusters) appear, we refit on the growing labelled set using the same prior-probability correction, re-estimate the spatial feature as new positives are confirmed (adding them to the distance target), and recompute the top-N dispatch list. Update frequency is tied to two clocks: the arrival rate (reports per month) and the biological season (queen emergence in spring, new-colony founding, fall dispersal).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let the labelled set at time t be L_t = {Positive, Negative records known by t}. Update rule: at each refresh, (1) add all newly labelled reports to L_t; (2) recompute the real class prior p_true(t) = n_pos/(n_pos+n_neg); (3) refit the logistic model on L_t (keeping the whole positive class, re-sub-sampling negatives to the same 1:20) and apply the prior-probability correction with p_true(t); (4) add any newly confirmed positives to the distance-to-positive target and recompute dist_to_positive_km for all open reports; (5) re-rank the open (unverified) reports and re-issue the top-N dispatch list. Reporting-rate data from the file: submissions per month rose from ~3-14/month (Jan-Mar 2020) to a peak of 1440/month (Aug 2020) then fell to 241/month (Oct 2020) — i.e. a seasonally and attention-driven surge. Given this cadence and the hornet's life cycle (fertilized queens emerge in spring, found colonies, new queens disperse in fall over ~30 km), the model should be refreshed at least monthly during the active season (April-October) and at every seasonal transition (spring emergence, fall dispersal), and triggered immediately upon any new confirmed positive (which moves the spatial feature and can shift the dispatch list within days). Between monthly refreshes the model is static; the daily task is only to score new arrivals with the current weights and append them to the dispatch queue.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: a concrete update policy — incremental refit on each newly labelled batch, with the class prior, the positive set (spatial feature), and the dispatch list all recomputed; refresh monthly in-season and at seasonal boundaries, plus an immediate trigger on any new confirmed positive. Interpretation: the monthly-in-season cadence matches both the reporting surge (up to ~1,440 reports/month, so a month accumulates enough new labels to materially shift the prior and the ranking) and the biology (the season in which queens found and disperse colonies). Limitations and biases: (1) the positive class stays tiny (14 at the data cutoff), so even monthly refits have a slowly-moving positive boundary — the prior correction dominates early and the text weights move only as positives accumulate; (2) if a new, distant introduction occurs, the spatial feature (distance to nearest *old* positive) is initially uninformative there, so the first few weeks at a new site rely on text alone — a lag the monthly cadence partly covers but not fully; (3) the report rate is attention-driven (spiked in 2020), so a 'steady' monthly assumption overstates the label flow in quiet months — in low-report months the update is effectively a no-op and the model simply waits.

tasks.task_description: Sub-problem 5: Using the model, specify what would constitute evidence that Vespa mandarinia has been eradicated in Washington State.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) under eradication (null hypothesis H0) the true VGH process has intensity zero, so no report is a genuine VGH; (b) reports keep arriving at the observed rate R (per month) even after eradication, because the public still files look-alike reports; (c) the model gives, for any report, the probability p that it is a true VGH, so the expected number of true positives in W months is lambda = W * R * p_true (a Poisson mean); (d) we want a confidence level (1 - alpha) that the absence of true detections is evidence of eradication rather than bad luck. Method: a Poisson 'zero-suffixed' / confidence-in-absence test. The probability of observing zero true positives over W months, given a residual true-positive rate, is exp(-lambda). We require this to be at least 1 - alpha, which bounds the tolerable residual mean lambda by -ln(1 - alpha), and hence bounds the required monitoring duration W.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let p_true = mean predicted probability a report is a true VGH (from the calibrated model, p_true ~ 2.7e-4 over the historical file) and R = reports/month. The expected true positives in W months of monitoring is lambda(W) = W * R * p_true. Eradication evidence at confidence 1 - alpha is: observe zero model-confirmed true VGH (i.e. every report classified true is subsequently lab-refuted, and no confirmed positive appears) for a duration W such that P(0 true | lambda) = exp(-lambda) >= 1 - alpha. Solving, W_min = -ln(1 - alpha) / (R * p_true). At the historical rate R ~ 444 reports/month (mean; peak 1,440) and p_true ~ 2.7e-4: at 95% confidence, -ln(0.05)=2.996, so W_min ~ 24.7 months; at 99% confidence, -ln(0.01)=4.605, so W_min ~ 37.9 months. Concretely: with the report flow and the model's per-report true-positive probability fixed, observing zero confirmed VGH for roughly 2-3 years (95%) to ~3 years (99%) — with the model continuously refuting look-alike reports — is the statistical evidence of eradication. A stricter, operationally stronger criterion: zero *confirmed* positives (lab-verified) for a full queen-generation cycle plus the 30 km dispersal season, i.e. no confirmed detection across at least one full spring-emergence-to-fall-dispersal season in every previously affected cluster, combined with the zero-true count above.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results: eradication evidence = a sustained run of zero model-confirmed true VGH long enough that the Poisson probability of having missed a residual population is below the chosen alpha. Quantitatively, at the historical report rate and per-report true-positive probability, that run is about 25 months for 95% confidence and about 38 months for 99% confidence; equivalently, no confirmed positive across at least one to two full biological seasons in all affected clusters. Interpretation: the threshold is set by the false-negative cost — because a single surviving queen can found a new colony 30 km away the next spring, 'eradicated' must mean 'we are confident no reproductive nest remains', and confidence in absence scales with how long and how thoroughly we kept finding nothing while the public kept reporting. Limitations and biases: (1) p_true and R are estimated from the 2019-2020 file, so the W_min is only as good as those estimates; if the public stops reporting after eradication, R falls and the zero-count becomes less informative (fewer opportunities to catch a survivor) — the duration should be extended when report volume drops; (2) the Poisson model assumes a constant residual rate, whereas a surviving queen produces a *seasonal* pulse (queens emerge in spring), so the strongest single piece of evidence is actually a silent *spring season* in a known cluster, not a uniform month count; (3) the test conditions on the model correctly labelling look-alikes as false — if the model's precision degrades, 'zero model-confirmed' is weaker evidence, which is why the operational criterion pairs the statistical run-length with lab-verified zero confirmations.
